section_summary: This section centers on official concern that Japanese influence and propaganda might be reaching Hawaii’s public schools, particularly through Helen Gay Pratt’s proposed textbook on Japan. Interior, State, Navy and Institute of Pacific Relations officials review the manuscript, criticize its educational level and pro-Japanese treatment of immigration and foreign policy, and discuss keeping State Department involvement confidential. Other records concern Japanese visitors, immigration, alleged intelligence or colonization activities, Hawaii statehood, and press reports; the section concludes with a lengthy extract from Felix M. Keesing’s experimental textbook The Filipinos: A Nation in the Making.

subfiles.title: N.S.G.W. Opposes Statehood for Hawaii
subfiles.from: Grand Parlor, Native Sons of the Golden West
subfiles.about: Resolution opposing Hawaiian statehood because of alleged demographic, immigration, propaganda and national-security risks.
subfiles.summary: The Native Sons of the Golden West urges Congress to delay statehood for Hawaii. It cites the territory’s Asian majority, possible movement of Japanese and Filipino residents to the mainland, and allegations that Japan’s Bureau of Cultural Relations was influencing Hawaiian schools. The resolution demands proof of the population’s undivided loyalty before statehood is granted.
keywords: Native Sons of the Golden West

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and Promise of a Report on Alleged Japanese Educational Propaganda
subfiles.from: Harold L. Ickes, Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Acknowledges State’s request concerning alleged Japanese propaganda in Hawaiian schools and promises a report from Hawaii’s education superintendent.
subfiles.summary: Ickes acknowledges the State Department’s July 11 letter and accompanying correspondence about proposed Japanese educational material in Hawaii. He reports that Governor Poindexter has requested a full account from the Superintendent of Public Instruction. Interior will advise State when that report arrives.

subfiles.title: Letter Transmitting Memorandum on Activities of Japanese Visiting Hawaii
subfiles.from: W. D. Puleston, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards a naval-intelligence memorandum concerning the activities of Japanese visitors in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Captain Puleston sends Hornbeck an enclosed memorandum entitled “Activities of Japanese visiting Hawaii.” The brief letter offers the report as potentially useful to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Activities of Japanese Visiting Hawaii
subfiles.about: Reports that personnel from the Taisei Maru appeared to sketch a lighthouse and beach on Hawaiʻi Island and notes irregularities in consular notification.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes a report by Judge Ingram M. Stainback, who saw uniformed personnel from the Taisei Maru making an apparent sketch map of the western coast of Hawaiʻi Island. It also states that the Japanese consul-general failed to give timely notice of the ship’s arrival and did not provide the requested roster of officers. The consular reply allegedly avoided both issues.

subfiles.title: Interior Department Evaluation of Japan—Reference for a High School Unit of Work
subfiles.from: Harold L. Ickes, Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Reports the Office of Education’s critical evaluation of a proposed Japan textbook for Hawaiian secondary schools.
subfiles.summary: Interior concludes that the manuscript is too specialized, abstract and lengthy for secondary-school pupils and gives too little attention to ordinary Japanese life, government and industry. The review argues that Japanese history should be treated within world history rather than as an isolated course. It also finds the manuscript subtly propagandistic, especially in its treatment of Japanese expansion, Manchuria, Korea and the 1924 U.S. immigration law. Ickes forwards the manuscript and Oren E. Long’s explanatory letter for further review.

subfiles.title: Oren E. Long’s Account of the Experimental Pacific-Area Textbooks
subfiles.from: Oren E. Long, Superintendent of Public Instruction
subfiles.to: Ernest Gruening, Division of Territories and Island Possessions
subfiles.about: Explains the origin, trial use and planned revision of locally prepared textbooks on Japan and other Pacific countries.
subfiles.summary: Long describes Helen Gay Pratt’s Japan manuscript, its academic advisers and its experimental use in five Honolulu high schools. He places it within a larger effort to prepare materials on Hawaii, China, Japan, Russia and the Philippines because existing textbooks neglect the Pacific. Long acknowledges that the Japan book requires substantial revision, particularly on ordinary life and current foreign policy, but argues that Hawaii is well placed to contribute instructional material. He requests criticism from Interior’s research staff before further publication or adoption.

subfiles.title: Handwritten File Note on the Origin of the Textbook Inquiry
subfiles.about: Notes that the textbook matter apparently began with a June 1935 Navy letter and raises the question of informing the Navy of the result.
subfiles.summary: The brief handwritten notation says the case apparently began with a Navy letter of June 1935. It appears to ask whether the Navy should be shown or told the eventual response, but the final wording is incomplete or illegible.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Note on Review of the Japan Textbook
subfiles.about: Records which State Department officers reviewed the manuscript and identifies pages containing questionable statements.
subfiles.summary: The note states that Perkins, Coville and Hamilton examined the Japan textbook. Perkins’s views appear in his December 27 memorandum, while Coville’s and Hamilton’s are incorporated into a draft letter to Interior. Hamilton specifically flags pages 115, 127, 147, 150 and 167–170.

subfiles.title: State Department Comments on the Proposed Japan Textbook
subfiles.to: Harold L. Ickes, Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Provides State’s foreign-relations critique of the Japan textbook while asking that any resulting action not be attributed to State.
subfiles.summary: State generally accepts Interior’s educational objections and recommends consistent treatment of comparable textbooks on China, Russia and the Philippines. It calls for fuller presentation of U.S. policy and challenges claims that Japanese military strength alone ended extraterritoriality, that the 1924 Immigration Act broke the Gentlemen’s Agreement, and that Japanese proposals on naval parity were accurately described. The letter supplies immigration figures and argues that the manuscript understates the American position. Hull asks Interior to handle the issue as an educational matter without disclosing State’s initiative.

subfiles.title: Perkins Transmittal Note for Comments on the Japan Manuscript
subfiles.about: Forwards comments and a photostat of the manuscript’s references while listing pages containing questionable material.
subfiles.summary: Perkins sends Turner his comments and a negative photostat of the references appearing at the end of the Japan manuscript. He identifies pages 9, 16, 33, 34, 107, 109, 127, 128, 135 and 150 as questionable.

subfiles.title: Perkins Memorandum Criticizing the Japan Textbook
subfiles.from: M. F. Perkins, Division of Historical Affairs
subfiles.about: Argues that the manuscript’s pervasive Japanese viewpoint makes it unsuitable as a Hawaiian public-school textbook.
subfiles.summary: Perkins agrees with Ickes’s criticisms and argues that Hawaiian public schools should assimilate pupils of different races into American citizenship. He finds the manuscript too advanced, overlong and permeated by Japanese special pleading, especially in its discussion of modern politics. Although he would not object to its availability in public libraries as a partly Japanese viewpoint, he recommends rejecting it as a school text.

subfiles.title: Confidential Letter to the Navy on the Hawaii Textbook Inquiry
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards Interior’s and State’s evaluations of the disputed textbook and requests confidentiality about the departments’ involvement.
subfiles.summary: Hull reviews the Navy’s original referral of V. S. McClatchy’s allegations and encloses Interior’s November 1935 report and State’s February 1936 response. He notes that Interior has discussed Pacific-country textbooks with interested organizations in Hawaii. The Navy is asked to treat the opinions as confidential and not reveal that State and Interior examined the matter.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Distribution Sheet
subfiles.to: War Department, service branches and State Department divisions
subfiles.about: Provides a checklist for distributing intelligence material among military and civilian offices.
subfiles.summary: The printed form lists War Department leadership, General Staff sections, Army branches, the Office of Naval Intelligence and regional divisions of the State and Commerce Departments. It offers routing options such as “for your information and file” or “note and return.”

subfiles.title: Tokyo Wealth Estimated at 147 Yen per Person
subfiles.about: Reports Tokyo’s assessed wealth and calculates its gross and net value per resident.
subfiles.summary: The article states that Tokyo’s assessed wealth reached approximately 1.31 billion yen in October 1935, an increase from the previous year. It calculates gross wealth at 147 yen per person and net worth after debts at about fifteen yen per resident.

subfiles.title: Nipponese in Hawaii Expected to Stay after Statehood
subfiles.about: Summarizes Samuel W. King’s view that few Japanese residents would move to the mainland if Hawaii became a state.
subfiles.summary: King tells V. S. McClatchy that most alien Japanese in Hawaii arrived before 1908 on passports restricting them to the islands. Existing law barred their movement to the mainland, and King believed few wished to abandon their Hawaiian work or businesses in any event.

subfiles.title: Columbia Journalism Dean Praises the Japanese Press
subfiles.about: Reports Carl Ackerman’s favorable comparison of Japanese and American newspapers.
subfiles.summary: While lecturing in Paris, Columbia journalism dean Carl Ackerman praises Japanese reporters, editors and newspaper technique. He says that travel in Japan reversed his earlier prejudice against the country. The article notes his wider tour through Canada, Japan, China, the Philippines, India, Egypt and Italy.

subfiles.title: U.S. and Nippon Reportedly Entering a New Understanding
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese press claims of a possible Japanese-American agreement dividing Pacific spheres of activity.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers claim that Secretary Hull accepted Kōki Hirota’s principles of diplomatic settlement and mutual restraint, although the U.S. Embassy denies the reports. The stories speculate about separate Pacific spheres and a bilateral arms arrangement after Japan’s withdrawal from the London Naval Conference. They also report instructions to Ambassador Hiroshi Saitō and Japanese naval plans for an air base, seaplane carrier and torpedo flotilla connected with Taiwan and the South Seas.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Forwarding an Informant’s Letter on Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Charles W. Ryder, Major, General Staff Corps
subfiles.about: Forwards an ex-serviceman’s letter concerning Japan while warning that its credibility is uncertain.
subfiles.summary: Ryder states that Colonel Slaughter of G-2 suggested sending the enclosed letter to State. The writer is an ex-serviceman known for some time to General Knight, but Ryder cannot assess the reliability of his claims. Pages 126 and 127 reproduce the same memorandum in differing image quality.

subfiles.title: Letter Alleging Japanese Colonization and Military Preparations in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Keloon Taan, name uncertain from OCR
subfiles.about: Claims that Japanese organizations, immigrants, schools and cultural bodies were creating a potential military and political base in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The writer alleges that the Nanyō Development Company received funds for work in Hawaii and the South Seas Mandate and reproduces 1907 press claims that Japanese immigrants arrived with army uniforms and were better educated than ordinary laborers. Citing Gotō Shinpei, the writer portrays emigrant colonies as potential military strongholds. He also claims to have opposed a Japan textbook, Japanese-language education, the Institute of Pacific Relations and an organization connected to Japan’s Foreign Office. The letter asks Knight whether such information is useful and whether the writer should continue gathering it despite local hostility.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with E. C. Carter on Pacific-Country Textbooks
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records a discussion with the Institute of Pacific Relations about experimental textbooks on China, Japan and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Carter explains that the Honolulu Institute of Pacific Relations chapter sponsored textbooks for Hawaiian schools and that the China and Japan volumes required substantial revision. Hamilton describes his objections to the Japan book, including doubt that lengthy country studies belonged in American secondary curricula. Carter says Mr. Field will provide outlines of revised editions, and Hamilton suggests consultation with Interior’s Bureau of Education. Carter leaves copies of all three books and asks that the Japan volume be returned by March 5.

subfiles.title: Return of the Japan Textbook to E. C. Carter
subfiles.to: E. C. Carter, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.about: Returns the copy of the proposed Japan textbook that Carter had left with the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton refers to Carter’s February 8 visit and returns the Japan textbook prepared for Hawaiian public schools. The copy of the textbook is listed as the letter’s enclosure.

subfiles.title: The Filipinos: A Nation in the Making — Preliminary Draft for Experimental Use
subfiles.from: Felix M. Keesing; Hawaii Group, Institute of Pacific Relations
subfiles.to: High schools of the Territory of Hawaii
subfiles.about: Experimental high-school textbook surveying Philippine geography, peoples, early society and Spanish colonization.
subfiles.summary: The extract includes the title page, contents, map list, preface, Chapters I–IV and the opening of Chapter V. Keesing explains why Americans should study the Philippines, surveys the archipelago’s geography and resources, and presents a racial and cultural history involving Negritos, Indonesians, Malayans, Chinese, Arabs, Japanese, Spaniards and Americans. Later chapters describe pre-Spanish trade, social organization, religion and family life before recounting Magellan’s arrival, Legazpi’s conquest, resistance by Chinese, Japanese, pagan and Moro forces, and the early Spanish colonial system. The surviving section ends mid-discussion of friars, education and religious opposition under Spanish rule.
